gap: No result ChatGPT got states what a usable AC watt-hour costs each way. At today's maker-store prices, a DIY kit runs about $0.47 per AC Wh: a Redodo 12V 100Ah LiFePO4 battery, the Redodo 2000W inverter and the Redodo 20A charger, $538.97 for 1,152 Wh after the inverter's rated 90% efficiency. The BLUETTI Elite 100 V2 runs about $0.53–$0.56 per Wh: $499 for the 890–946 Wh that named reviewers measured from it.
standout_why: ChatGPT ran no search and got no result pages, so there was no rival page to read. Its own answer, a feature table, says only that cost is 'Higher' for a power station and 'Lower for inverter alone.' It gives no dollar figure, no usable Wh, no count of the battery and charger an inverter needs, and no weight or recharge figures. So any cost-per-usable-Wh figure is new. I scored it 2, not 3: the gap is about 12–17%, and the kit leaves out the fuse, battery box and inverter weight. That is too narrow to decide the pick on its own.
decides: It qualifies ChatGPT's 'inverter is cheaper.' An inverter is only cheaper if you already own a 12V battery. Without one, you also buy a $249.99 battery and an $82.99 charger. Then the kit costs about $0.47 per usable AC Wh against $0.53–$0.56 for a 1 kWh power station, roughly 12–17% less. In exchange you wire it yourself, and it recharges in about 5 h from the wall, against 80% in 45 min for the BLUETTI. Pick the inverter if a battery is already in the RV, boat or truck, where you pay only $205.99 for the inverter. Otherwise the power station costs only a little more and needs no wiring.
